We exclude stocks priced below $5 per share to ensure that our results are not driven by micro-cap or illiquid firms.
To be included in our sample for a given month, we require that at least 15 daily stock return observations are available to calculate the key variables.
we define MAX as the average of the five highest daily returns generated by a stock in a given month.

We construct $ \text{MAX}^\beta $ by first sorting stocks into decile portfolios based on their market beta, and then within each beta-sorted portfolio, we sort stocks into decile portfolios based on their MAX. We then group together all stocks with the same MAX portfolio ranking, $ n $, across the different beta portfolio ranks, and call the newly formed decile portfolio the $ \text{MAX}^\beta $ portfolio of rank $ n $.
A stock’s market beta at the end of each month is estimated as the slope coefficient from a regression of its daily excess returns on the market’s excess returns over a 252-day rolling window.
Market capitalization (SIZE) is a stock’s number of shares outstanding multiplied by its price per share.

The book value of a firm is calculated as the sum of stockholders’ equity (SEQ), deferred taxes (TXDB), and investment tax credit (ITCB), minus the book value of preferred stock (PSTKRV, PSTKL, or PSTK).
BM is the natural logarithm of the ratio of a firm’s book value to its market capitalization.
intermediate-term momentum (MOM) is measured as a stock’s cumulative return over the 11-month period prior to the portfolio formation month.
Short-term reversal (REV) is the excess return generated over the portfolio formation month (Jegadeesh, 1990).
a stock’s monthly illiquidity (ILLIQ, scaled by $10^6$) is the ratio of the daily absolute stock return to the dollar trading volume averaged over the past one month.
Asset growth is the change in the book value of assets scaled by lagged assets.
Return-on-equity is income before extraordinary items (IBQ) divided by one-quarter-lagged book equity.

Idiosyncratic volatility (IVOL) is computed as the standard deviation of the daily residuals from regressing a stock’s daily excess returns on the market’s excess returns over a 252-day rolling window, using the same specification employed to estimate market beta.

Institutional holdings (INST) data are from the Thomson Reuters Institutional Holdings (13F) database. INST measures the percentage of a firm’s shares held by institutional investors at each quarter-end.

We test the significance of the return spreads on MAX- and MAX $ ^{\beta} $ -sorted portfolios using a comprehensive set of factor models: (i) CAPM with the excess market return (MKT); (ii) Fama-French (1993) three-factor (FF3) model with the MKT, size (SMB), and book-to-market (HML) factors; (iii) Fama-French-Carhart four-factor (FFC4) model with the MKT, size (SMB), book-to-market (HML), and Carhart’s (1997) momentum factor; (iv) FFCPS model that combines the FFC4 model with the liquidity factor of Pastor and Stambaugh (2003); (v) Fama-French (2015) five-factor (FF5) model with the MKT, size (SMB), book-to-market (HML), profitability (RMW), and investment (CMA) factors; (vi) Fama-French (2018) six-factor (FF6) model that combines the FF5 model with the momentum factor; and (vii) the 7-factor model (FF6PS) that combines the FF6 model with the liquidity factor of Pastor and Stambaugh (2003).

MAX $ ^{\text{Treynor}} $ scales the magnitude of extreme returns by systematic risk and is calculated as the average of the five highest daily returns in a month (MAX) divided by the stock’s market beta.
we sort stocks in ascending order based on their MAX values, defined as the average of the five highest daily returns in a given month, and form 10 decile portfolios.

We restrict our Fama–MacBeth analyses to a fixed sample in which all observations have available data for every independent variable: MAX, BETA, MIS, CE, SIZE, BM, REV, MOM, ILLIQ, ROE, I/A, and IVOL.

The winsorization procedure applied here would not affect the portfolio-level tests, which constitute the majority of the analyses carried out in the paper, as the portfolios are created according to their characteristics ranks (such as the ones for MAX and MAX $ ^{\beta} $) and their granularity is above a percentile.
We select this sample period [April 1980 to December 2022] as it represents the broadest timeframe for which all firm characteristics used in our analysis are concurrently available.
